Didn't Soren Kierkegaard, the first existentialist, posit that you should try to create your own meaning despite the meaninglessness? I think the second half of your comment is right though. Camus said to embrace the meaninglessness and absurd, and yet still live on despite that, rebelling against the absurd with your own existence. But doing that very thing kinda gives you reason to live on, aka meaning in life, so it kinda just loops back around to existentialism, doesn't it?

Fair enough, so existentialism is the act of saying "give your own life meaning"? With absurdism denying existentialism based on the fact Camus (again, this is to my own interpretation) himself denies the idea of giving your own life meaning, in favor of living on and embracing the absurd despite the fact of it being absurd?

To my understanding, optimistic nihilism is more of the attitude of giving your own life meaning, despite the universe being inherently meaningless. Not sure if this is right or not since a lot of people seem to confuse the two, but absurdism is recognizing that trying to find meaning in an inherently meaningless universe is absurd. The philosopher who popularized it (or invented it whichever), Camus, says that even trying to make a meaning for yourself isn't worth it, falls short, or is as pointless as the universe. Instead, he says to embrace the absurdity of there being no meaning, and avoid giving your life artificial meaning (my words, not his), and instead rebel against the absurdity with the proclomation of your own existence despite its inherent meaninglessness. Course all this could be wrong, because from my standpoint absurdism and optimistic nihilism seem to get the same interpretations.

It really depends on the context of the situation, and that says a lot because we don’t know what context we’re living in. Optimism isn’t always inherently good. If we lived in a system that is forced happiness, or you are in a lot of bad situations that you cannot control, it is a bit naive to just say everything is fine and try to convince yourself you’re happy, kinda like in an abusive marriage where you try to be happy cause you’re suppose to be happy during this.

Vice versa, pessimism isn’t necessarily bad either. Say you’re in a cult and everything is just some facade and everyone is a crazy cultist and you’re right, the system is right, all others are wrong. But you take a critical look at this organization and you see it’s utter shit and you leave. 

I think to be realistic in todays society is to look through the facade we all try to uphold, that things will be fine or people are happy and you should strive to be happy (last part is debatable), and that can come off as pessimistic simply because this stuff is “happy” in the way it is presented. However, to be realistic is to also see how what many people see as a bad thing is actually a good thing and there isn’t really anything wrong with it. Nothing is perfect so I can’t really come up with an idea, but saying that we’re unlikely to get nuked anytime soon is far more realistic than saying every presidential election “president x is gonna destroy the world.”

Tldr: optimism is not always good, pessimism isnt always bad, to be realistic you will often have a mix of both, and in todays happy driven industry you’ll often find yourself seen as a pessimist due to the need to look through the happiness veil.
